content: Dracunculiasis, commonly referred to as Guinea worm disease (GWD), is an infection caused by the parasitic nematode Dracunculus medinensis. This parasite is also known as the Guinea worm, Medina worm, or fiery serpent, with the latter name reflecting the Latin root Dracunculus, meaning little dragon. The life cycle of the Guinea worm begins when a female worm emerges through the skin of its human host approximately one to two years after the initial infection. Individuals with emerging worms often enter drinking water sources, inadvertently allowing the worm to release larvae into the water. These larvae are ingested by microscopic freshwater arthropods called copepods, or water fleas, particularly those of the genus Cyclops. Within the copepods, the larvae develop into their infectious stage over 10 to 14 days. Humans become infected by consuming water containing these infected copepods. Once inside the human body, stomach acid digests the copepod but not the Guinea worm larvae it harbors. The larvae migrate to the small intestine and then into the body cavity. Over the next 10 to 14 months, the female worm mates with a male worm. The male, which is much smaller, dies and is absorbed into the host's body. The female worm grows to its full length of 60–100 centimeters (2–3 feet) and a width comparable to a cooked spaghetti noodle. The adult female becomes packed with thousands of tiny larvae. The worm migrates to the area of the body where it will emerge, which in over 90% of cases is one of the lower limbs. A blister forms on the skin at the site of emergence, causing an intense burning sensation. Within 24 to 72 hours, the blister ruptures, exposing one end of the worm. To alleviate the burning sensation, infected individuals often immerse the affected limb in water. When the blister, now an ulcer or open sore, is submerged, the adult female worm releases a milky white fluid containing hundreds of thousands of larvae into the water. Over the following days, the worm can continue releasing larvae whenever it comes into contact with water, thereby contaminating the water supply and perpetuating the disease's life cycle. Diagnosis of dracunculiasis often involves imaging studies. Radiographs may reveal calcified Guinea worms, which are common findings in endemic areas. Studies have shown that 89% of patients with calcified worms are asymptomatic. Treatment of dracunculiasis typically involves the manual extraction of the worm by slowly winding it around a stick. This method, which has been practiced for millennia, may have inspired the Rod of Asclepius, a symbol of the medical profession. The process begins when the worm starts to emerge from the skin. It is carefully wound around a stick, a few centimeters at a time, over the course of several days or weeks. This slow extraction is necessary to avoid breaking the worm, as leaving a portion of the dead worm inside the host can increase the risk of secondary infection and trigger immune responses, causing pain and swelling. In some countries, broken worms are immediately removed surgically. Where facilities are available, surgical excision of the worm may be performed from the outset. Adjunctive therapy with medications such as metronidazole or thiabendazole in adults can facilitate the extraction process. However, one study found that anthelmintic therapy was associated with aberrant migration of worms, leading to infections in areas other than the lower extremities. Therefore, such medications should be used cautiously. If dracunculiasis is suspected based on history or clinical findings, consultation with an infectious disease specialist is recommended for management and follow-up care. This also allows for the initiation of epidemiologic protocols if the patient presents in a non-endemic country. Efforts to eradicate dracunculiasis have been spearheaded by the Dracunculiasis Eradication Program (DEP), funded by organizations such as the Carter Center and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. As of 2005, Asia has been declared free of dracunculiasis, and transmission has been interrupted in 9 of the 20 countries where eradication efforts began. By 2004, fewer than 50 cases were reported in five endemic countries. The DEP set a goal of global eradication by 2009. The number of cases has dramatically decreased from 3.5 million in 1986 to approximately 16,000 in 2004. Currently, dracunculiasis occurs only in 12 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, with transmission most common in remote rural villages and areas frequented by nomadic groups. Historically, the disease was described as early as the 2nd century BCE by the Greek writer Agatharchides, who noted its prevalence among nomads in what is now Sudan and along the Red Sea. In 2004, countries such as Ghana, Sudan, and Nigeria reported 7,275, 7,266, and 495 cases of GWD, respectively. Other endemic countries reported fewer cases, including Benin (3 cases), Burkina Faso (60 cases), Côte d'Ivoire (21 cases), Ethiopia (17 cases), Mali (357 cases), Mauritania (13 cases), Niger (293 cases), and Togo (278 cases). Kenya and Uganda reported imported cases from Sudan. Transmission no longer occurs in several African countries, including Kenya, Senegal, Cameroon, Chad, and the Central African Republic. The World Health Organization has certified 180 countries as free of dracunculiasis transmission, including five formerly endemic countries: Pakistan (1996), India (2000), Senegal (2004), Yemen (2004), Cameroon (2007), and the Central African Republic (2007). The significance of an infection reported in a country considered free of dracunculiasis depends on the species of the parasite. Occasionally, zoonotic species such as D. insignis, which typically infect animals, may infect humans. These cases are atypical and not a cause for concern. However, infection by D. medinensis in a location considered GWD-free is of great concern to eradication efforts. Differentiating between the human parasite D. medinensis and other Dracunculus species is crucial. This can be achieved through examination of the patient’s travel history and DNA fingerprinting of the worm. Prevention of GWD relies on simple control measures, as the disease is transmitted exclusively through drinking contaminated water. These measures include drinking only water from uncontaminated underground sources, such as boreholes or hand-dug wells; preventing individuals with open Guinea worm ulcers from entering drinking water sources; filtering drinking water using cloth or nylon mesh filters to remove water fleas; treating unsafe water sources with approved larvicides like Abate; and providing communities with new safe drinking water sources or repairing dysfunctional ones.
